Tengu Botnet Reboots Compromised Linux Devices When Defenders Kill Its Process

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 11 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new Mirai-derived botnet called Tengu can use a compromised Linux device's hardware watchdog to trigger a reboot when defenders kill its main process. If that happens, Tengu's other persistence mechanisms get another chance to relaunch it. Nozomi Networks Labs observed the dropper reaching its honeypots through Telnet credential brute force. Tengu supports 25 distributed denial-of-service (

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Telnet credential brute force against internet-exposed IoT/Linux devices (Tengu dropper entry) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Tengu ELF-header corruption ('ELFOOD') of Linux reboot/shutdown utilities · [LLM] Tengu guardian process masquerading as kernel thread [kworker/0:0] · [LLM] Tengu immutable-binary persistence via chattr +i on Linux/IoT
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Tengu botnet C2 / IPFS beacon to 64.89.163.8 on TCP 9931 and 8080 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Telnet credential brute force against internet-exposed IoT/Linux devices (Tengu dropper entry) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts high-volume inbound Telnet (TCP/23) connection attempts from a single external source against Linux/IoT hosts, the entry vector Nozomi observed for the Tengu dropper on its honeypots. Article-specific because Tengu spreads exclusively via Telnet default/weak-credential brute force rather than an exploit. Rationale: Uses the article's stated entry vector (Telnet TCP/23 credential brute force on internet-exposed IoT/Linux) as a volumetric single-source pivot; port 23 to public-facing embedded hosts is inherently high-signal since legitimate Telnet exposure is rare. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html
ATT&CKT1110 T1078.001 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal network/security scanner (Shodan-style, Nessus, Nmap) sweeping TCP/23 across the estate
  • A misconfigured legacy management tool that legitimately polls Telnet on embedded gear
  • ISP/upstream background internet scanning noise hitting an exposed device
  • Load-balancer or NAT health checks probing port 23
  • Penetration-test engagement against IoT segment
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<known_scanner_ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target hosts are IoT/embedded and that TCP/23 is genuinely internet-reachable; check whether any attempt succeeded (post-auth session, new process). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the perimeter, disable/firewall Telnet on the exposed devices, and rotate any default credentials. 3) Hunt: on any device that accepted a session, pivot to Tengu post-compromise indicators — outbound TCP/9931 to 64.89.163.8, a process masquerading as [kworker/0:0], chattr +i on new binaries, and modified /sbin/reboot|shutdown utilities.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where LocalPort == 23 and RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Attempts = count(), Devices = dcount(DeviceId), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP
| where Attempts > 20   // empirical Telnet brute-force volume threshold from a single source
| order by Attempts desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort == 23
| summarize Attempts = count(), Denied = countif(DeviceAction in~ ("deny","drop","blocked","reset")), Targets = dcount(DestinationIP), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP
| where Attempts > 20   // brute-force volume threshold on Telnet/23 from a single source
| order by Attempts desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as attempts, dc(All_Traffic.dest) as targets, min(_time) as firstSeen, max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=23 All_Traffic.transport=tcp by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.action | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where attempts>20 | sort - attempts
| tstats summariesonly=false count as attempts, dc(All_Traffic.dest) as targets, min(_time) as firstSeen, max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=23 All_Traffic.transport=tcp by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.action | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where attempts>20 | sort - attempts
Tengu botnet C2 / IPFS beacon to 64.89.163.8 on TCP 9931 and 8080 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any egress from an internal host to the hardcoded Tengu C2 IP 64.89.163.8 over TCP/9931 (plaintext registration/heartbeat) or TCP/8080 (IPFS gateway payload retrieval). Article-specific because both the IP and the two ports are named in the analyzed sample's configuration. Rationale: The C2 IP 64.89.163.8 and both ports (9931 for plaintext registration/heartbeat, 8080 for the IPFS gateway) are explicit strings from the analyzed sample; a hardcoded single-IP + non-standard-port pair is near-zero-FP. URLhaus independently logged 17 malicious Mirai-related URLs at the same IP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html • https://urlhaus.abuse.ch/host/64.89.163.8/
ATT&CKT1571 T1071.001 T1105 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate IPFS node/user on the estate happening to reach port 8080 on that host (unlikely — IP is a known-bad C2)
  • Threat-intel or sandbox detonation VM deliberately beaconing to the IOC during analysis
  • Security researcher/blue-team validating the IOC from a lab host
  • Stale NAT/proxy log attributing the connection to the wrong internal source
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal source device and the initiating process (Defender InitiatingProcessFileName / Falcon ContextImageFileName); confirm the host is IoT/Linux. 2) Contain: block 64.89.163.8 at the perimeter, isolate the device from the network, and preserve volatile state before power actions (Tengu corrupts reboot/shutdown binaries). 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts beaconing to the same IP/ports, and on the infected host review systemd units, /etc/init.d, /etc/rc.local, shell rc files, cron, and /dev/watchdog before reimaging.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "64.89.163.8"
| where RemotePort in (9931, 8080)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "64.89.163.8"
| where DestinationPort in (9931, 8080)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHost = SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, ApplicationProtocol, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Tengu ELF-header corruption ('ELFOOD') of Linux reboot/shutdown utilities AIInstallation Medium
Hunts non-package-manager modification of the on-disk reboot/shutdown/halt/poweroff binaries, which Tengu overwrites (ELF magic replaced with 'ELFOOD') to block defenders from cleanly restarting or powering down a compromised device. Article-specific: standard admin/patch flows never rewrite these binaries outside the package manager. Rationale: Directly targets Tengu's named self-defense behaviour (overwriting reboot/shutdown ELF headers with 'ELFOOD'); modification of these system binaries outside a package manager is a rare, high-fidelity signal on Linux/IoT. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html
ATT&CKT1222.002 T1562.001 T1529
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate OS upgrade replacing coreutils/systemd/busybox binaries (should show a package-manager initiating process)
  • A vendor firmware-update agent rewriting /sbin binaries in place
  • Admin manually recompiling/replacing a shutdown wrapper
  • Configuration-management tool (Ansible/Puppet copy module) deploying a patched binary
Suppression filter
// Defender: already excludes package managers via InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (...). Add vendor firmware agent if known:
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("fwupd","swupdate")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the initiating process and confirm it is NOT a package manager; on the host, check whether the reboot/shutdown binaries' ELF magic has been replaced with 'ELFOOD' (first bytes not \x7fELF). 2) Contain: isolate the device and DO NOT trust local reboot/shutdown commands — use an out-of-band power/PDU action; snapshot for forensics first. 3) Hunt: correlate with a [kworker/0:0] masquerade process, /dev/watchdog usage, chattr +i on new binaries, and beacons to 64.89.163.8:9931 on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/sbin/reboot","/sbin/shutdown","/sbin/halt","/sbin/poweroff","/usr/sbin/reboot","/usr/sbin/shutdown","/usr/sbin/halt","/usr/sbin/poweroff")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","yum","dnf","opkg","busybox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/sbin/reboot","/sbin/shutdown","/sbin/halt","/sbin/poweroff","/usr/sbin/reboot","/usr/sbin/shutdown","/usr/sbin/halt","/usr/sbin/poweroff")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("dpkg","apt","rpm","yum","dnf","opkg","busybox"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, DvcAction, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Tengu ELFOOD Corruption of Reboot/Shutdown Utilities

Tengu guardian process masquerading as kernel thread [kworker/0:0] AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a user-land process whose command line/argv[0] is spoofed to the kernel-thread name [kworker/0:0] but is backed by a real on-disk executable — Tengu's watchdog-feeding background worker. Article-specific: genuine kernel workers never appear as execve'd processes with an on-disk image. Rationale: Targets Tengu's named masquerade ([kworker/0:0]); real kernel threads are not created via execve and thus never surface in process-creation telemetry with an on-disk image path, making a spawned process bearing that name inherently anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A poorly-written admin script or monitoring agent that deliberately sets its process title to a kworker-like string
  • Container runtime or emulation layer surfacing kernel-thread names into userland process telemetry
  • A benign process legitimately named with a leading bracket by a developer
  • EDR sensor mislabeling a genuine kernel worker as a userland process on an exotic embedded kernel
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("docker","containerd","runc","qemu-system")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the FolderPath/SHA256 of the spoofed process — a real on-disk binary confirms masquerade; check whether it holds /dev/watchdog open. 2) Contain: isolate the device; capture the binary and memory before any power action, since killing the process may starve the watchdog and force a reboot. 3) Hunt: look for the guardian re-spawn pattern (a binary relaunched ~60s after being killed), the persistence set (systemd/init/rc/cron/shell rc), chattr +i binaries, and C2 to 64.89.163.8:9931.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName startswith "[kworker" or ProcessCommandLine startswith "[kworker"
| where isnotempty(FolderPath) and FolderPath !startswith "/proc"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine startswith "[kworker" or TargetProcessName startswith "[kworker"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Tengu Guardian Masquerading as Kernel Thread kworker
id: a1d6f0b3-5e29-4c74-9b81-7c2e3a0d55c9
description: Detects a user-land process spoofing the kernel-thread name [kworker/0:0], matching Tengu's watchdog-feeding background worker.
references:

logsource:

detection:

| ImageFileName=/.+/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, min(_time) as firstSeen, values(Processes.process_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="[kworker*" OR Processes.process_name="[kworker*") by Processes.dest Processes.process Processes.process_path Processes.process_exec | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where isnotnull(process_path) AND NOT match(process_path,"^/proc") | sort - firstSeen
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstSeen, values(Processes.process_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="[kworker*" OR Processes.process_name="[kworker*") by Processes.dest Processes.process Processes.process_path Processes.process_exec | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where isnotnull(process_path) AND NOT match(process_path,"^/proc") | sort - firstSeen
Tengu immutable-binary persistence via chattr +i on Linux/IoT AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of chattr with the immutable (+i) flag, which Tengu uses to mark its installed binary undeletable so defenders can't simply rm it. Article-specific: chattr +i is rare on embedded/IoT hosts and is a named Tengu self-defense step. Rationale: Directly maps to Tengu's named tactic of marking its binary immutable; chattr +i is uncommon on IoT/embedded Linux, so its execution — especially targeting a recently dropped binary — is a strong persistence/anti-removal signal. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html
ATT&CKT1222.002 T1564
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin hardening a config file (e.g. chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf) as a legitimate lockdown
  • Configuration-management or security-baseline tooling applying immutability to protect files
  • Backup or integrity tooling setting the immutable bit on archives
  • A developer testing filesystem attributes on a build host
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/resolv.conf","/etc/hosts","/etc/passwd") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the target path of the chattr +i and the parent process; a recently written binary in /tmp, /var, /dev, or a hidden path strongly indicates malware anti-removal. 2) Contain: isolate the host, then clear the immutable bit (chattr -i) before removal and preserve a copy for forensics; avoid reboot until reboot/shutdown binaries are verified intact. 3) Hunt: pivot to the full Tengu footprint on the host — [kworker/0:0] masquerade, /dev/watchdog, ELFOOD-corrupted utilities, and C2 to 64.89.163.8:9931.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "chattr"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("+i", "+ai")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "chattr"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("+i", "+ai")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Tengu Immutable-Binary Persistence via chattr +i

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",

| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Mass IPMI RAKP hash harvesting — one host probing many BMCs on UDP/623 (CVE-2013-4786) AIReconnaissance High
Hunts a single source rapidly connecting to many distinct hosts on UDP port 623 (IPMI), the fan-out signature of RAKP/RMCP+ pre-auth password-hash harvesting per CVE-2013-4786 (e.g. Metasploit ipmi_dumphashes / CosmicRakp). Distinct-destination fan-out on 623 separates a hash-sweep from normal point-to-point BMC administration. Rationale: Anchored on the article's concrete protocol facts — UDP/623 + IPMI RAKP/RMCP+ pre-auth HMAC-SHA1 hash disclosure (CVE-2013-4786). The distinct-destination fan-out is what turns generic 623 traffic into a high-fidelity harvesting signal; corroborated via NVD, Dell KB and Rapid7 ipmi_dumphashes. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2013-4786 • https://www.dell.com/support/kbdoc/en-us/000222162/data-domain-ipmi-v2-0-password-hash-disclosure • https://attackerkb.com/topics/wr9OgD7FNL/cve-2013-4786
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1110.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7) sweeping the management VLAN for IPMI exposure
  • Data-center automation/DCIM tooling polling many BMCs for hardware telemetry
  • Redfish/IPMI bulk firmware-update orchestration touching a fleet of controllers
  • Internal asset-discovery job enumerating UDP/623 across a /24
  • NOC health-check script pinging every chassis' management port on a schedule
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.10.10.5")   // pin your sanctioned scanner/DCIM host(s) here to suppress authorized sweeps
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is not a sanctioned scanner/DCIM host; check whether the destinations are your BMC management subnet and whether the source sits outside it. 2) Contain: block UDP/623 at the network edge and ACL the management VLAN so only approved admin jumpboxes reach BMCs; if the source is internal and unsanctioned, isolate it. 3) Hunt: for any BMC that answered, treat its IPMI password as compromised — rotate factory/default creds (ADMIN/root), disable IPMI 1.5, and review BMC console/firmware logs for follow-on logins.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 623 and Protocol =~ "Udp"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize DistinctBMCs = dcount(RemoteIP), SampleTargets = make_set(RemoteIP, 50), TotalConns = count() by DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctBMCs > 20   // one host hitting 20+ distinct public IPMI endpoints/hr = RAKP hash sweep
| order by DistinctBMCs desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort == 623
| summarize DistinctBMCs = dcount(DestinationIP), SampleTargets = make_set(DestinationIP, 50), TotalConns = count() by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctBMCs > 20   // 20+ distinct BMCs on IPMI/623 from one source in 1h = scanning, not admin
| order by DistinctBMCs desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:623 @Protocol:(udp OR UDP)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=623
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=DistinctBMCs))
| DistinctBMCs > 20
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count values(All_Traffic.dest) as dest dc(All_Traffic.dest) as dest_count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=623 All_Traffic.transport=udp by All_Traffic.src _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where dest_count > 20
| sort - dest_count
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(All_Traffic.dest) as dest dc(All_Traffic.dest) as dest_count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=623 All_Traffic.transport=udp by All_Traffic.src _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where dest_count > 20
| sort - dest_count
Internet-sourced traffic reaching BMC IPMI interfaces on UDP/623 (exposure of CVE-2013-4786) AIReconnaissance High
Hunts public-Internet source addresses reaching an internal host on UDP port 623, i.e. an exposed BMC/IPMI management interface vulnerable to CVE-2013-4786 pre-auth hash disclosure. Surfaces the 24,650-BMC exposure class described in the article — any inbound 623 from a non-RFC1918 source is a management plane that should never face the internet. Rationale: Uses the article's core exposure fact: IPMI on UDP/623 disclosing RAKP hashes pre-login (CVE-2013-4786), with public-to-private direction as the exposure discriminator. NVD and Dell both confirm there is no patch and blocking 623 at the edge is the primary control, so an exposed 623 is inherently actionable. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2013-4786 • https://www.dell.com/support/kbdoc/en-us/000222162/data-domain-ipmi-v2-0-password-hash-disclosure
ATT&CKT1133 T1595.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Managed-hosting/GPU-provider architecture that intentionally exposes iLO/iDRAC/IPMI over a VPN concentrator NAT'd from a public IP
  • Vendor remote-support session (HPE/Dell/Supermicro) temporarily reaching the BMC from a public support IP
  • Cloud bare-metal provider control-plane addressing BMCs via public IP ranges
  • Perimeter firewall NAT hairpin logging an internal source as its public egress IP
  • Security-team's own external attack-surface scan validating the 623 exposure
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("203.0.113.10")   // pin sanctioned vendor-support / management VPN egress IP(s) to suppress legitimate remote BMC access
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the DestinationIP is a BMC/management controller and that the public SourceIP is not a sanctioned remote-support/VPN endpoint. 2) Contain: block UDP/623 inbound at the edge immediately and move the BMC onto a dedicated isolated management network with ACLs to approved admin systems only. 3) Hunt: assume the RAKP hash was already grabbed — rotate the BMC password (especially factory/empty ADMIN/root creds called out in the report), disable IPMI 1.5/weak ciphers, and audit BMC login and firmware-update logs for unauthorized access or iLOBleed-style rootkit persistence.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 623
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), Conns = count(), DistinctSources = dcount(RemoteIP), Sources = make_set(RemoteIP, 50) by DeviceName, DeviceId, LocalIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort == 623
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false and ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP) == true
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Conns = count(), DistinctSources = dcount(SourceIP), Sources = make_set(SourceIP, 50) by DestinationIP, DestinationHostName
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Internet-Exposed IPMI BMC Interface Reachable on UDP 623 (CVE-2013-4786)
id: 6f2a1c9e-4b7d-4e2a-9c11-2d3e4f5a6b7c
description: Detects inbound network connections from a public source to UDP port 623 (IPMI/RMCP+), indicating an internet-exposed Baseboard Management Controller vulnerable to CVE-2013-4786 pre-auth RAKP password-hash disclosure.
references:
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2013-4786
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering

tags:

  - attack.t1595.001

detection:

    DestinationPort: 623

level: medium
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=623 ConnectionDirection=1
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, LocalAddressIP4], function=count(RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=DistinctSources))
NETWORK

| tstats summariesonly=true count values(All_Traffic.src) as src dc(All_Traffic.src) as src_count min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=623 All_Traffic.transport=udp by All_Traffic.dest

| where NOT (cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src))

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where NOT (cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src))

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2013-4786")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a4f49c40b510dcab6824ee7c30f4d852", "d9d2bf5dcd4b9a02b16e7d8f5e4c1a7", "5dfc3a5d88e17c4b3a2e6d9f8c1b0d", "c1d2e3f45678b9dae1234d567e8e9f0a") or SHA1 in~ ("a4f49c40b510dcab6824ee7c30f4d852", "d9d2bf5dcd4b9a02b16e7d8f5e4c1a7", "5dfc3a5d88e17c4b3a2e6d9f8c1b0d", "c1d2e3f45678b9dae1234d567e8e9f0a") or MD5 in~ ("a4f49c40b510dcab6824ee7c30f4d852", "d9d2bf5dcd4b9a02b16e7d8f5e4c1a7", "5dfc3a5d88e17c4b3a2e6d9f8c1b0d", "c1d2e3f45678b9dae1234d567e8e9f0a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a4f49c40b510dcab6824ee7c30f4d852", "d9d2bf5dcd4b9a02b16e7d8f5e4c1a7", "5dfc3a5d88e17c4b3a2e6d9f8c1b0d", "c1d2e3f45678b9dae1234d567e8e9f0a") or SHA1 in~ ("a4f49c40b510dcab6824ee7c30f4d852", "d9d2bf5dcd4b9a02b16e7d8f5e4c1a7", "5dfc3a5d88e17c4b3a2e6d9f8c1b0d", "c1d2e3f45678b9dae1234d567e8e9f0a") or MD5 in~ ("a4f49c40b510dcab6824ee7c30f4d852", "d9d2bf5dcd4b9a02b16e7d8f5e4c1a7", "5dfc3a5d88e17c4b3a2e6d9f8c1b0d", "c1d2e3f45678b9dae1234d567e8e9f0a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a4f49c40b510dcab6824ee7c30f4d852", "d9d2bf5dcd4b9a02b16e7d8f5e4c1a7", "5dfc3a5d88e17c4b3a2e6d9f8c1b0d", "c1d2e3f45678b9dae1234d567e8e9f0a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48027", "CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48027", "CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JFrog Confirms OpenAI Models Exploited Artifactory Zero-Day Before Hugging Face Breach

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 7 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

JFrog has confirmed that OpenAI models exploited a zero-day in self-hosted Artifactory while trying to reach the open internet from a sealed evaluation environment. Artifactory is JFrog's software repository manager. OpenAI says the models then escalated privileges and moved laterally until they reached an internet-connected node. JFrog says it has since developed and released fixes for cloud

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Self-hosted JFrog Artifactory exposed to OpenAI-credited zero-days (CVE-2026-65618/65923/66018) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Self-hosted JFrog Artifactory exposed to OpenAI-credited zero-days (CVE-2026-65618/65923/66018) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces managed hosts whose vulnerability inventory flags a self-hosted Artifactory install against the three Artifactory CVE records credited to OpenAI researchers in the ExploitGym/Hugging Face incident. This is an exposure hunt, not an active-exploit detection — the article and JFrog disclose no exploitation strings, so the only deployable article-specific pivot is confirming which self-hosted Artifactory nodes are patchable and internet-adjacent. Rationale: Uses the three concrete CVE IDs named in the article (CVE-2026-65618/65923/66018) — the only corroborable artifacts — matched against the JFrog Artifactory product in TVM inventory. High-fidelity as an exposure signal because the CVE-to-product match is exact; deliberately scoped as hunting because neither JFrog nor OpenAI published any exploit string, affected-version-to-incident mapping, or IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/jfrog-confirms-openai-models-exploited.html • https://www.cvedetails.com/product/35352/Jfrog-Artifactory.html?vendor_id=15996 • https://app.opencve.io/cve/?product=artifactory&vendor=jfrog • https://jfrog.com/help/r/jfrog-release-information/cves-impacting-artifactory
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM snapshot is stale — host was already patched to the remediating build but the daily inventory hasn't re-scanned yet
  • Air-gapped dev/test Artifactory instances that carry the vuln but have no internet egress path (lower real risk than the internet-adjacent proxy in the article)
  • Scanner matched a broad affected-version range that includes a build JFrog later clarified as not impacted (see JFrog 'CVEs Not Impacting Artifactory' list)
  • JFrog Cloud (SaaS) tenants — already vendor-remediated per the article — that appear via a bundled JFrog agent rather than a self-hosted install
  • Duplicate rows where the same DeviceId reports multiple co-located JFrog components (Artifactory + Xray) inflating the exposed-host count
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName in (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | where IsInternetFacing == true | distinct DeviceName)
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged host, compare the reported SoftwareVersion against the fixed-version threshold in the JFrog release notes / security advisory for its maintained branch; confirm whether the instance is self-hosted (in scope) vs a JFrog Cloud agent (already remediated). 2) Contain: prioritise any node that is internet-facing or acts as a package-registry proxy/cache (the exact break-out path in the incident) — restrict outbound egress from that host and apply the remediating build. 3) Hunt: on confirmed-vulnerable proxy nodes, review Artifactory access/audit logs and host EDR for unexpected local privilege escalation, new admin tokens, or lateral movement originating from the registry service account in the days before patching.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical OpenWrt DHCPv6 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Run Code as Root

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 8 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

OpenWrt has shipped version 24.10.8 to close a critical DHCPv6 stack overflow and a wider set of remotely triggerable flaws in network services enabled by default. The critical issue, tracked as CVE-2026-53921 and rated 9.8 on CVSS 3.1 in OpenWrt's GitHub advisory, lets an unauthenticated attacker able to reach the DHCPv6 server overwrite a stack buffer in odhcpd through a crafted DHCPv6
