| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Inbound FastJson @type payload with jar:/ldap:/rmi: reference to Spring Boot app (CVE-2026-16723) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP request bodies/URIs carrying a FastJson '@type' key alongside a nested jar:, ldap:, rmi: URL or JdbcRowSetImpl/dataSourceName reference — the exploitation shape for CVE-2026-16723 against internet-facing Spring Boot fat-JAR apps. Article-specific because it keys on the @type + remote-resource-lookup combination, not generic deserialization. Rationale: Keys on the CVE-2026-16723 exploitation signature — a FastJson '@type' key co-occurring with a jar:/ldap:/rmi: remote-resource URL or the JdbcRowSetImpl/dataSourceName lookup class — confirmed by Imperva's advisory and the public jsontype RCE lab. Only expressible on WAF/proxy telemetry that captures request bodies; endpoint EDR/FDR do not ship HTTP bodies, hence Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.imperva.com/blog/imperva-customers-protected-against-cve-2026-16723-critical-fastjson-1-x-zero-day-rce/ • https://github.com/alibaba/fastjson2/wiki/Security-Advisory:-Remote-Code-Execution-in-fastjson-1.2.68%E2%80%931.2.83 • https://github.com/dinosn/fastjson-jsontype-rce-lab
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / DAST tools (Burp, Nessus, Nuclei) probing for fastjson with @type test payloads
  • Legitimate APIs that accept a client-supplied field literally named 'type' where the value contains a jar: or ldap: URI
  • Internal red-team / BAS (Picus, SafeBreach) exercises replaying deserialization payloads
  • Log-shipping of stored @type strings in JSON documents that are echoed back into request URLs
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestURL has_any ("nuclei","nessus") or Message has_any ("nuclei","nessus") or SourceIP in ("10.0.0.0/8"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request from the WAF/proxy for the matched SourceIP; confirm the body contains @type plus a remote jar:/ldap:/rmi: URL and identify the DestinationHostName Spring Boot app and its FastJson version (1.2.68-1.2.83?). 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, enable FastJson SafeMode (-Dfastjson.parser.safeMode=true) on the target app, and isolate the app host if outbound class-load already occurred. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'Java outbound LDAP/RMI' and 'Java fat-JAR spawning shell' on the destination host within a 5-minute window of the request to confirm code execution.

Spring Boot Java fat-JAR spawning shell/recon child process (FastJson CVE-2026-16723 RCE) AIExploitation High
Detects a Java process launched as a Spring Boot executable fat-jar (java -jar xxx.jar) spawning cmd/powershell/sh/bash or a recon binary — the post-exploitation payload of CVE-2026-16723 landing on the app server. Article-specific: it requires the '-jar' parent context Alibaba names as the sole deployment prerequisite. Rationale: Anchors on Alibaba's stated prerequisite — a Spring Boot executable fat-jar (java -jar xxx.jar) — as the parent, paired with a shell/recon child, which is the concrete RCE outcome of CVE-2026-16723. Parent+child pairing keeps FP low versus a bare java or bare powershell query. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fastjson-1x-rce-vulnerability-targeted.html • https://github.com/alibaba/fastjson2/wiki/Security-Advisory:-Remote-Code-Execution-in-fastjson-1.2.68%E2%80%931.2.83 • https://github.com/dinosn/fastjson-jsontype-rce-lab
ATT&CKT1190 T1203 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Jenkins/GitLab/TeamCity build agents (Java) legitimately invoking sh/bash/cmd for build steps
  • Java-based application servers shelling out to certutil/curl for cert or health-check tasks
  • Elastic/Logstash Java agents spawning helper processes
  • Admins running gradlew/mvnw wrappers that fork shells from a java parent
  • Monitoring tooling (Java) calling nslookup/ping for connectivity checks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jenkins","gitlab-runner","teamcity","elastic-agent","logstash") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gradlew","mvnw"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture InitiatingProcessCommandLine to confirm the fat-jar name and whether the child cmdline shows recon/download (whoami, curl to external IP); correlate with any inbound @type WAF hit on the same host within minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the app server, kill the java parent, and apply FastJson SafeMode or migrate to fastjson2 (no vendor patch exists). 3) Hunt: on the same host review DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound LDAP/RMI (UC below) and any dropped .class/.jar in temp, and sweep the fleet for the same fat-jar name running vulnerable FastJson 1.2.68-1.2.83.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","whoami.exe","whoami","net.exe","curl.exe","curl","wget","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","nslookup.exe","ping.exe","id","uname")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe","/java")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","/sh","/bash","/dash","whoami","net.exe","curl","wget","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","nslookup.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Java application making outbound LDAP/RMI connection (FastJson CVE-2026-16723 remote class load) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects a java -jar process initiating an outbound connection to LDAP (389/636), RMI registry (1099) or the JNDI-exploit-kit LDAP port (1389) on a public host — the attacker-controlled resource lookup FastJson performs before AutoType checks, pulling a malicious class. Article-specific: ties the egress to a Spring Boot fat-JAR process on JNDI/RMI ports. Rationale: Corroborated detection indicator from Imperva/the PoC lab: outbound LDAP/RMI from an app server to an unexpected external host is the JNDI/defineClass remote class-load step. Scoping to a java -jar process on JNDI/RMI ports keeps this high-fidelity; a directory-bound corporate LDAP server is normally internal, not public. Cross-checked against: • https://www.imperva.com/blog/imperva-customers-protected-against-cve-2026-16723-critical-fastjson-1-x-zero-day-rce/ • https://github.com/dinosn/fastjson-jsontype-rce-lab • https://medium.com/@pa2sw0rd/deep-dive-into-fastjson-deserialization-vulnerabilities-from-principles-to-practical-defense-c3be134ec8a6
ATT&CKT1105 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Java app authenticating users against an external/cloud-hosted LDAP directory (e.g. some managed AD/LDAP)
  • Java RMI microservices calling a partner RMI registry over 1099
  • Legacy apps configured with a public LDAP endpoint for address-book lookups
  • Vulnerability scanners generating JNDI callbacks during authorized testing
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP != "" and not (RemoteIP startswith "10." or RemoteIP startswith "192.168." or RemoteIP matches regex @"^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[0-1])\.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP — is it a known corporate/cloud LDAP or an unfamiliar external host/VPS? Check the fat-jar name and whether a shell child spawned on the same host within seconds. 2) Contain: block egress to the RemoteIP on JNDI/RMI ports from server subnets, isolate the host, and enable FastJson SafeMode on the app. 3) Hunt: capture any class file the JVM fetched, pivot to process-tree UC for java-spawned shells, and enumerate other hosts running FastJson 1.2.68-1.2.83 fat-jars that egressed to the same IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (389, 636, 1099, 1389)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActionType has "Connection"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where RemotePort in (389, 636, 1099, 1389)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] VeloCloud Orchestrator web service spawning shell for DB export / archive / egress (CVE-2026-16812)

Inbound connection from known CVE-2026-16812 exploitation IPs to VCO web interface AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound TCP/HTTP(S) connections to the VeloCloud Orchestrator management interface originating from the three IP addresses Arista attributed to active exploitation of the unauthenticated command-injection zero-day. Any hit is a direct IOC match against confirmed attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the three exploitation IPs published in the Arista advisory (verbatim in SA-0144 and CISA KEV) — a direct infrastructure IOC match with no behavioural inference required. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices/security-advisory/24364-security-advisory-0144 • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanner or CTI provider that happens to reuse one of these IPs for benign scanning (rare, verify with reverse DNS)
  • Shared-hosting IP later reassigned to a legitimate service after Arista's observation window
  • Internal red-team sourcing from an IP that collides with the IOC set
  • Threat-intel platform test/heartbeat traffic replaying IOC lists
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination is a VCO management host and pull the corresponding web access log lines for the source IP — look for encoded chars / internal-service path components around the connection time. 2) Contain: block the three IPs at the perimeter, restrict the VCO web interface to admin networks only, and snapshot logs + filesystem timestamps before any remediation. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same VCO host for web-service→shell process spawns (UC2) and unexpected outbound egress (UC3); if confirmed, treat the appliance as compromised — patch is insufficient, rotate all credentials/certs/keys and validate managed Edge devices.

VeloCloud Orchestrator web service spawning shell for DB export / archive / egress (CVE-2026-16812) AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation signature of the VCO OS command-injection flaw: the orchestrator's web tier (nginx/Node.js/Java) spawning a Unix shell or data-handling tool that runs a database dump, archive creation, or outbound fetch. Directly targets Arista's 'unexpected command execution, file creation, database exports, or archive files' IOC guidance. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CWE-78 exploitation outcome Arista called out (unexpected command execution, database export, archive files) by requiring a web-tier parent process spawning a shell/dump/archive/egress tool — a combination that essentially never occurs on a healthy orchestrator appliance. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices/security-advisory/24364-security-advisory-0144
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scheduled DB backup job legitimately invoking mysqldump/pg_dump under a web-service account (verify cron/systemd-timer parentage, not a web-request-driven spawn)
  • Appliance health/telemetry scripts calling curl/wget to Arista update endpoints
  • Vendor support engineer running diagnostic tar/gzip during a maintenance session
  • In-product config-export feature shelling out to tar (validate against expected admin action)
  • Node.js app legitimately spawning sh for a documented internal maintenance task
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("cron","crond","systemd","systemd-cron") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "/etc/cron"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and command line — confirm the parent is the web-facing service and whether the shell ran a DB dump, archive, or egress; correlate the timestamp with inbound web requests (UC1) and access-log anomalies. 2) Contain: isolate the VCO host from the network, kill the offending process, and preserve logs + filesystem timestamps before remediation. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written/archived and any outbound transfers (UC3); if a dump/archive left the host, assume compromise of managed device inventories, credentials, certs and keys — rotate everything and validate/replace the appliance rather than relying on the patch alone.

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mysqldump","pg_dump","tar ","zip ","gzip","curl ","wget ","/dev/tcp/","base64","nc ","ncat ")
    or FileName in~ ("mysqldump","pg_dump","pg_dumpall","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256

Unexpected outbound egress from VeloCloud Orchestrator host (C2 / data exfil) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts outbound HTTP(S)/TCP initiated by the VCO host — either back to the three known exploitation IPs, or by a web-service/shell process reaching a public address. An orchestrator normally receives management connections, so service-account egress to the internet indicates reverse-shell C2 or exfil of the exported database/archive. Rationale: Combines Arista's 'unexpected outbound HTTP/HTTPS from the VCO host' guidance with the three attributed IPs and a service/shell-process egress filter, so the detection fires on reverse-shell C2 or exfil of the dumped DB even when the destination differs from the published IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices/security-advisory/24364-security-advisory-0144 • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VCO reaching Arista/VMware update, licensing, or telemetry endpoints over HTTPS (baseline and allowlist the legitimate FQDNs)
  • NTP/DNS or monitoring-agent egress from the appliance to approved public resolvers
  • Node.js app calling an approved external API (e.g. cloud object storage for legitimate backups)
  • Package-manager (apt/yum) update traffic during a maintenance window
  • Proxy/NAT collapsing many hosts onto the VCO source IP inflating the egress picture
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has "arista.com" and RemoteUrl !has "velocloud.net" and RemoteUrl !has "vmware.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the egress destination and the initiating process/command line — is it a known Arista endpoint or an unfamiliar public IP; check bytes-out for bulk transfer consistent with a DB/archive exfil. 2) Contain: block the destination and the three IOC IPs, cut the appliance's outbound internet path, and capture a memory/disk snapshot before remediation. 3) Hunt: tie the egress back to a web-service→shell spawn (UC2) and inbound exploit-IP hits (UC1) to confirm the full chain; if exfil is confirmed, rotate all VCO-managed credentials, certificates and cryptographic keys and validate every managed Edge device for tampering.

// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-16812")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Dysphoria botnet blockchain C2 resolution via ENS/SNS (.eth/.sol) domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts hosts resolving or connecting to the Dysphoria/JackSkid blockchain naming-service C2 records (m3rnbvs5d.eth, burrberry.eth, 24carnforth2merseyside.sol) or any .eth/.sol pseudo-TLD used to encode distribution-node IPv4 addresses. Blockchain name resolution on IoT/enterprise gear is highly abnormal and is the botnet's headline resilience mechanism. Rationale: Anchored on the three concrete blockchain C2 records named by XLab/CNCERT and cross-confirmed by BleepingComputer and GBHackers; .eth/.sol resolution is near-zero baseline on corporate/IoT segments, making the pseudo-TLD hunt high-fidelity as well as the exact-domain match. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/ • https://gbhackers.com/dysphoria-iot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1568 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web3/blockchain developer workstations resolving ENS/SNS names via eth.limo or eth.link gateways
  • MetaMask or other crypto wallet browser extensions performing ENS lookups
  • DeFi/NFT research or trading endpoints in fintech orgs
  • Security researchers detonating samples in an internal sandbox
  • IPFS gateways that proxy .eth content addresses
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and RemoteUrl has_any ("eth.limo","eth.link"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving asset — if it is an IoT device, router, camera or Linux edge box with no legitimate crypto function, treat as compromised; capture InitiatingProcess and the resolved IPv4. 2) Contain: block the .eth/.sol domains and any resolved distribution-node IPs at the egress firewall and isolate the device from the internet. 3) Hunt: pivot on the resolved IPs (see distribution-node UC), search the same segment for Telnet/SSH scanning fan-out and UPnP port-mapping bursts, and sweep all IoT subnets for additional .eth/.sol resolvers.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol")
    or RemoteUrl endswith ".eth" or RemoteUrl endswith ".sol"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol")
    or Name endswith ".eth" or Name endswith ".sol"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Answer = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Dysphoria IoT Botnet Blockchain C2 Domain Resolution (ENS/SNS)
id: 9c1f2a44-7b3e-4c6a-9d21-8e5f0a3b1c77
description: Detects DNS resolution of Dysphoria/JackSkid blockchain naming-service C2 records or any .eth/.sol pseudo-TLD used to hide distribution-node IPv4 addresses.
references:

  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/

      - '24carnforth2merseyside.sol'

#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(m3rnbvs5d\.eth|burrberry\.eth|24carnforth2merseyside\.sol|\.(eth|sol))$/i

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution where DNS.query IN ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol","*.eth","*.sol") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer DNS.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Egress to Dysphoria distribution-node / relay IPs (194.87.198.x, 194.58.38.x) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any monitored host connecting to the five Dysphoria distribution-node IPv4 addresses that the ENS/SNS records resolve to and that infected relays forward traffic through. These are named campaign IOCs so a hit is high-confidence C2/relay activity. Rationale: The five IPs are the pre-extracted campaign IOCs and correspond to the HTTP-served distribution nodes/relays described by XLab (confirmed by GBHackers/BleepingComputer); a direct-IP match needs no behavioural context to be actionable. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/dysphoria-iot-botnet/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) reaching the IPs during a scheduled scan
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance actively probing published IOCs
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse where the address later serves a benign service
  • Security researcher sandbox traffic egressing through the corporate perimeter
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("scanner","nessus","qualys") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nessusd","qualys-cloud-agent"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm direction and initiating process/asset; a low-privilege IoT/edge device beaconing to these IPs is a confirmed relay/bot. 2) Contain: block the five IPs at egress, quarantine the source device, and preserve any /tmp payloads for the malware team. 3) Hunt: correlate the source with .eth/.sol resolution and Telnet/SSH scanning UCs, and check whether the host is also serving inbound public connections (relay role).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("194.87.198.208","194.87.198.104","194.58.38.79","194.58.38.49","194.58.38.96")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("194.87.198.208","194.87.198.104","194.58.38.79","194.58.38.49","194.58.38.96")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Dysphoria Botnet Distribution-Node C2 IP Connection
id: 3a7d6e12-4f88-4b0c-a1e9-2c4b7f9d5e30
description: Detects outbound connections to the five Dysphoria/JackSkid distribution-node and relay IPv4 addresses published by XLab and CNCERT.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/dysphoria-iot-botnet-adds-blockchain-c2.html
  - https://gbhackers.com/dysphoria-iot-botnet/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/28
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1571
logsource:
  category: network_connection
detection:
  selection:
    DestinationIp:
      - '194.87.198.208'
      - '194.87.198.104'
      - '194.58.38.79'
      - '194.58.38.49'
      - '194.58.38.96'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Threat-intel or vulnerability scanners probing the same IPs
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:(194.87.198.208 OR 194.87.198.104 OR 194.58.38.79 OR 194.58.38.49 OR 194.58.38.96)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=/^(194\.87\.198\.(208|104)|194\.58\.38\.(79|49|96))$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip IN ("194.87.198.208","194.87.198.104","194.58.38.79","194.58.38.49","194.58.38.96") by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip IN ("194.87.198.208","194.87.198.104","194.58.38.79","194.58.38.49","194.58.38.96") by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Compromised device Telnet/SSH weak-password worm fan-out AIDelivery Medium
Detects a single internal host initiating outbound connections to many distinct public destinations on TCP/23 (Telnet) or TCP/22 (SSH) — the credential-guessing worm-spread behaviour XLab and CNCERT call the botnet's most consistent way in. High distinct-destination fan-out on these ports is the signature of a newly infected node scanning for the next victim. Rationale: Both published lists agree weak Telnet/SSH credential guessing is the primary propagation channel; distinct-destination fan-out on 22/23 from one source is the cleanest network expression of that worm behaviour without needing per-device auth logs the IoT gear won't ship. Threshold is aggregation-based so no single-event Sigma is emitted. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/dysphoria-iot-botnet/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1021.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Nmap) sweeping SSH/Telnet across a range
  • Ansible/SaltStack/Puppet config-management pushing to many hosts over SSH
  • IT jump/bastion host with legitimate broad SSH reach
  • Network monitoring platform probing device availability on 22/23
  • Backup or patch-orchestration appliance connecting to many managed devices
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("bastion","jump","scanner","ansible","nessus","qualys") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nmap","nessusd","ssh","sshpass","ansible"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: is the source a sanctioned scanner/bastion/config-mgmt host? Check the initiating process and whether targets are internal (admin) or public (worm scan) — public fan-out from an IoT/edge device is malicious. 2) Contain: block outbound 22/23 from the device, isolate it, and rotate any credentials it could have brute-forced. 3) Hunt: check the same host for .eth/.sol resolution and distribution-node IP egress; sweep destinations it hit for successful logons indicating fresh compromise.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort in (22, 23)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(RemoteIP), SampleTargets = make_set(RemoteIP, 25), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where DistinctTargets >= 30   // 30 = worm-scan fan-out floor; normal client SSH/Telnet hits <5 distinct public hosts/day
| order by DistinctTargets desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort in (22, 23)
| where CommunicationDirection =~ "Outbound" or isempty(CommunicationDirection)
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationPort
| where DistinctTargets >= 30   // worm-scan fan-out floor
| order by DistinctTargets desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:(22 OR 23)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=22 OR RemotePort=23) ConnectionDirection=1
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true))
| _count >= 30
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as distinct_targets min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (22,23) All_Traffic.direction="outbound" by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where distinct_targets >= 30 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - distinct_targets
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as distinct_targets min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (22,23) All_Traffic.direction="outbound" by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where distinct_targets >= 30 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - distinct_targets
Dysphoria relay node: public-to-public traffic bridging (UPnP port-forwarding relay) AICommand & Control Low
Hunts the relay-only Dysphoria variant that drops DDoS modules and turns a device into a proxy, using UPnP to create ~155 gateway port-forwarding rules and Linux epoll to shuttle traffic between an inbound internet connection and a remote C2. Surfaces monitored hosts that simultaneously accept many inbound public connections and open many outbound public connections — the traffic-symmetry signature of a relay bridge. Rationale: Anchored on XLab's June relay-only variant that uses UPnP (155 port-forwarding rules, per BleepingComputer) and epoll to bridge an inbound internet connection to a remote C2; the detectable enterprise signature is one host with high inbound-public AND high outbound-public connection cardinality. Confidence is Low because IoT relays rarely emit EDR telemetry and legit reverse proxies share the shape — treat as a triage-list hunt, not an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/ • https://gbhackers.com/dysphoria-iot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1090.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate reverse proxies / load balancers (NGINX, HAProxy) fronting public services
  • VPN concentrators or SASE gateways terminating and forwarding sessions
  • Corporate NAT gateway or SD-WAN edge bridging many flows
  • Public-facing jump/bastion host with broad inbound and outbound reach
  • CDN or caching appliance in a DMZ
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has_any ("proxy","lb","haproxy","nginx","vpn","gateway","bastion","edge")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is a sanctioned proxy/gateway/LB; an IoT device, camera, router or unmanaged Linux box exhibiting relay symmetry is suspect — inspect for miniupnpd/UPnP AddPortMapping bursts and unexpected listeners. 2) Contain: remove the device's UPnP port mappings on the gateway, block its inbound exposure, and isolate it. 3) Hunt: pivot the host's outbound peers against the distribution-node IP and .eth/.sol UCs, and enumerate the gateway for the ~155 forwarding rules characteristic of this variant.
let Window = 1d;
let Inbound = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Window)
    | where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | summarize InboundPublic = dcount(RemoteIP) by DeviceId, DeviceName;
let Outbound = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Window)
    | where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionRequest")
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | summarize OutboundPublic = dcount(RemoteIP) by DeviceId;
Inbound
| join kind=inner Outbound on DeviceId
| where InboundPublic >= 10 and OutboundPublic >= 10   // relay bridges public<->public on one node
| project DeviceName, InboundPublic, OutboundPublic
| order by InboundPublic desc
let Window = 1d;
let Inb = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
    | where NetworkDirection =~ "Inbound"
    | where ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr) == false
    | summarize InboundPublic = dcount(SrcIpAddr) by DvcHostname;
let Outb = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
    | where NetworkDirection =~ "Outbound"
    | where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
    | summarize OutboundPublic = dcount(DstIpAddr) by DvcHostname;
Inb
| join kind=inner Outb on DvcHostname
| where InboundPublic >= 10 and OutboundPublic >= 10
| project DvcHostname, InboundPublic, OutboundPublic
| order by InboundPublic desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ConnectionDirection=0 RemoteAddressIP4=/^(?!10\.|192\.168\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.)/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true))
| _count >= 10
| join({#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ConnectionDirection=1 RemoteAddressIP4=/^(?!10\.|192\.168\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.)/ | groupBy([aid], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true)) | _count >= 10}, field=aid)
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(All_Traffic.src_ip) as inbound_sources from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction="inbound" by All_Traffic.dest_ip | rename All_Traffic.dest_ip as host | where inbound_sources >= 10 | append [| tstats `summariesonly` dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as outbound_dests from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction="outbound" by All_Traffic.src_ip | rename All_Traffic.src_ip as host | where outbound_dests >= 10] | stats values(inbound_sources) as inbound_sources values(outbound_dests) as outbound_dests by host | where isnotnull(inbound_sources) AND isnotnull(outbound_dests)
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.src_ip) as inbound_sources from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction="inbound" by All_Traffic.dest_ip | rename All_Traffic.dest_ip as host | where inbound_sources >= 10 | append [| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as outbound_dests from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction="outbound" by All_Traffic.src_ip | rename All_Traffic.src_ip as host | where outbound_dests >= 10] | stats values(inbound_sources) as inbound_sources values(outbound_dests) as outbound_dests by host | where isnotnull(inbound_sources) AND isnotnull(outbound_dests)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("194.87.198.208", "194.87.198.104", "194.58.38.79", "194.58.38.49", "194.58.38.96") or RemoteUrl has_any ("m3rnbvs5d.eth", "burrberry.eth", "24carnforth2merseyside.sol")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["194.87.198.208", "194.87.198.104", "194.58.38.79", "194.58.38.49", "194.58.38.96"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["m3rnbvs5d.eth", "burrberry.eth", "24carnforth2merseyside.sol"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Machine account creation by low-privileged user (Certighost ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota stepping stone) · [LLM] AD CS CA server initiating SMB/LDAP to a non-DC host (Certighost rogue chase endpoint) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New Certighost PoC exploit lets attackers hijack Windows domains
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Machine account creation by low-privileged user (Certighost ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota stepping stone) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the first step of the Certighost (CVE-2026-54121) chain: a non-privileged domain user creating one or more computer accounts under the default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota. The attacker needs a valid machine principal to satisfy the CA's chase-endpoint authentication, so a low-priv user minting machine accounts is an early, article-specific tell. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit statement that 'a low-privileged user first creates a machine account, which is permitted under the default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota setting.' Event 4741 with a non-machine SubjectUserName is the earliest deterministic footprint of the chain. Cross-checked MSRC advisory and the H0j3n gist writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2026-54121 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/certighost-exploit-lets-low-privileged.html
ATT&CKT1136.002 T1078.002
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SCCM/MDT/autopilot provisioning accounts joining workstations (should be machine or known service accounts)
  • Helpdesk staff pre-staging computer accounts before domain join
  • Cloud sync connectors (Azure AD Connect) writing device objects
  • Lab/imaging technicians bulk-creating test computer accounts
  • Automation running under a delegated user rather than a service account
Suppression filter
| where SubjectUserName !in~ ("svc-domainjoin","svc-sccm","svc-autopilot")   // append tenant-known provisioning service accounts once validated
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SubjectUserName is a standard user (not helpdesk/provisioning). Pull the new TargetUserName machine account and check ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota consumption and whether the account has SPNs or DNS host records. 2) Contain: disable the freshly created machine account and the creating user; block cert enrollment from that principal at the CA. 3) Hunt: pivot to CA 4886/4887 enrollment events and 4768 PKINIT TGTs referencing any DC$ within the following hour to confirm the full Certighost chain.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4741            // A computer account was created
| where isnotempty(SubjectUserName)
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"     // exclude machine/DC-driven provisioning
| where SubjectUserName !in~ ("SYSTEM","ANONYMOUS LOGON")
| summarize NewMachineAccounts = make_set(TargetUserName), AccountsCreated = dcount(TargetUserName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName, Computer
| where AccountsCreated >= 1     // 1 = surface all; raise to >=2 for burst-creation alerting
| order by AccountsCreated desc

AD CS CA server initiating SMB/LDAP to a non-DC host (Certighost rogue chase endpoint) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the Certighost chase redirection: the Enterprise CA (certsrv.exe) is coerced into contacting an attacker-controlled SMB/LSA/LDAP listener supplied via the cdc request attribute. Flags first-seen outbound 445/389/636 connections from the CA service to hosts it has never previously authenticated against. Rationale: Anchored on 'the CA connects to the server specified in the cdc value' and 'run rogue SMB, LSA, and LDAP services.' certsrv.exe (the AD CS CA service) reaching a host it never previously authenticated against on 445/389/636 is the chase redirection. Sentinel left empty: process-attributed CA egress lives in MDE DeviceNetworkEvents / Sysmon EID3, not in a clean Sentinel ASIM/SecurityEvent shape in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/27/certighost-cve-2026-54121-poc-exploit-released/
ATT&CKT1187 T1649
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CA replicating/authenticating to a newly promoted domain controller not yet in the 30-day baseline
  • CA host querying a new certificate publication point or CDP/AIA server
  • Backup or monitoring agent on the CA opening SMB to a new file server
  • Load-balanced/multi-homed DC presenting a new IP
  • CA joining a new AD site with fresh DC connectivity
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP — is it a legitimate domain controller (DNS SRV, ntds) or an unmanaged workstation/attacker host? Check whether the destination corresponds to a recently created machine account (link to UC1). 2) Contain: isolate the CA server from the suspect host, and pause certificate issuance (stop CertSvc) if abuse is confirmed. 3) Hunt: review 4886/4887 CA request logs for requests carrying cdc/rmd attributes and any DC$ subject in the same window; validate the July 2026 patch (chase validation) is installed.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(RecentWindow)

| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "certsrv.exe"     // AD CS CA service process

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

BleepingComputer
2026-07-27 6 use cases 1 technique 2 kill-chain phases detected

The Coca-Cola Company has confirmed that hackers stole data from its dairy subsidiary, Fairlife, during a ransomware attack earlier this month. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Anubis ransomware execution via distinctive /WIPEMODE /PFAD= /KEY= command-line flags
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anubis ransomware Volume Shadow Copy deletion via hardcoded /for=norealvolume artifact · [LLM] Anubis ransomware mass file encryption — .anubis extension write burst · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Anubis ransomware execution via distinctive /WIPEMODE /PFAD= /KEY= command-line flags AIInstallation High
Hunts the Anubis ransomware payload (family that hit Coca-Cola's Fairlife subsidiary) by its unique command-line switch set. Anubis requires operator-supplied flags — /KEY= to start encryption, /elevated to self-escalate, /PFAD= to exclude paths, /PATH= to target a directory, and /WIPEMODE to irreversibly zero files instead of encrypting. The /WIPEMODE and German-language /PFAD= tokens are near-unique to this family. Rationale: Uses the Anubis-specific CLI switches /WIPEMODE, /PFAD= (German 'Pfad'=path), /KEY= and /elevated documented by Trend Micro; /WIPEMODE and /PFAD= are effectively unique to this family, making this very high fidelity even absent hashes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/anubis-ransomware-adds-wiper-to-destroy-files-beyond-recovery/ • https://blog.barracuda.com/2025/07/11/wipe--leak--extort--the-crazy-hybrid-playbook-of-anubis-ransomwa
ATT&CKT1486 T1485 T1548
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backup or archival tool that happens to use a /KEY= licensing argument together with an /elevated relaunch flag
  • Custom internal admin scripts that pass a /PATH= directory argument (mitigated — this rule requires /PFAD= or /WIPEMODE specifically)
  • Security-team detonation of Anubis samples in a sandbox/lab host
  • Red-team or purple-team ransomware simulation using the real Anubis binary
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.manager.exe","backup.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "/WIPEMODE" and ProcessCommandLine !has "/PFAD=")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent process; confirm the binary is unsigned/newly-dropped and check the SHA256 against Trend Micro Anubis IOCs. Note whether /WIPEMODE is present — if so recovery is impossible, treat as destructive. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host immediately via EDR, kill the process tree, and block the binary hash org-wide; alert IR lead given active encryption/wiping. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same SHA256/parent across all hosts, look for the paired vssadmin norealvolume shadow-copy deletion and mass .anubis file renames on this and neighbouring hosts, and review recent RDP/WinRM logons to the host for the ingress account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/WIPEMODE","/PFAD=")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "/KEY=" and ProcessCommandLine has "/elevated")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has_any ("/WIPEMODE","/PFAD=")
   or (CommandLine has "/KEY=" and CommandLine has "/elevated")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Anubis Ransomware Command-Line Flags
id: 5b7c1e2a-9f3d-4a1c-8b6e-2d4f7a9c1e30
description: Detects Anubis ransomware payload execution by its distinctive /WIPEMODE, /PFAD= and /KEY=+/elevated command-line switches
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/coca-cola-confirms-data-theft-in-fairlife-ransomware-attack/
  - https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:
  - attack.t1486
  - attack.t1485
  - attack.t1548
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_wipe:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/WIPEMODE'
      - '/PFAD='
  selection_key:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '/KEY='
      - '/elevated'
  condition: selection_wipe or selection_key
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@CommandLine:(*/WIPEMODE* OR */wipemode* OR */WipeMode*) OR @CommandLine:(*/PFAD=* OR */pfad=*) OR (@CommandLine:(*/KEY=* OR */key=*) AND @CommandLine:(*/elevated* OR */ELEVATED*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/\/(WIPEMODE|PFAD=)/i OR (CommandLine=/\/KEY=/i AND CommandLine=/\/elevated/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*/WIPEMODE*" OR Processes.process="*/PFAD=*" OR (Processes.process="*/KEY=*" AND Processes.process="*/elevated*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Anubis ransomware Volume Shadow Copy deletion via hardcoded /for=norealvolume artifact AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Anubis's pre-encryption inhibit-recovery step. The payload shells out 'vssadmin delete shadows /for=norealvolume /all /quiet' — the literal placeholder volume 'norealvolume' is a hardcoded Anubis artifact that distinguishes it from routine vssadmin shadow maintenance. Rationale: The full string 'vssadmin delete shadows /for=norealvolume /all /quiet' is documented by Trend Micro as Anubis's exact shadow-copy deletion command; the bogus 'norealvolume' volume name is a hardcoded artifact absent from any legitimate admin usage, giving near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html • https://www.securityweek.com/anubis-ransomware-packs-a-wiper-to-permanently-delete-files/
ATT&CKT1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None realistic for the 'norealvolume' token — it is not a real volume so no legitimate admin or backup product supplies it
  • A malware analyst re-running the Anubis binary in a lab
  • Purple-team ransomware emulation deliberately reproducing the Anubis vssadmin string
  • A YARA/AV signature test harness echoing the command into a log without executing it
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is a high-confidence hit — confirm the parent process (the ransomware payload) and its SHA256, and check whether encryption/.anubis renames have already begun on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host via EDR now, kill the parent process tree, and disable the executing account; shadow copies are already gone so prioritise stopping spread over local recovery. 3) Hunt: search all hosts for the same parent hash, the /WIPEMODE|/PFAD= command lines, and .anubis file writes; check backup infrastructure and hypervisors (ESXi/Nutanix) for the same actor given Anubis's cross-platform VM targeting.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "delete shadows" and ProcessCommandLine has "norealvolume"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\vssadmin.exe"
| where CommandLine has "delete shadows" and CommandLine has "norealvolume"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anubis ransomware mass file encryption — .anubis extension write burst AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the impact stage where Anubis appends the .anubis extension to encrypted files (or zeroes them in wiper mode). Aggregates file writes/renames to .anubis per host and process so a single encrypting binary touching many files fires once, not per file. Rationale: Anubis appends the .anubis extension to encrypted files (Trend Micro); a burst of >50 distinct .anubis writes from one process on one host is textbook mass-encryption impact and cleanly distinguishes ransomware from any legitimate single-file usage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html • https://www.bitsight.com/blog/anubis-ransomware-group-overview-and-evolution
ATT&CKT1486 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A researcher extracting an Anubis sample set where files are already named *.anubis (mitigated by the >50-distinct-path threshold plus single-process grouping)
  • Backup/AV quarantine that copies encrypted victim files preserving the .anubis name (would show a backup-agent parent, not the ransomware binary)
  • Threat-intel repo sync that writes many .anubis IOC sample files to a security team share
  • DFIR evidence collection copying an encrypted volume onto an analysis host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.manager.exe","msmpeng.exe","backup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm InitiatingProcess/ContextImageFileName is an unsigned recently-dropped binary (not a backup or AV agent) and check FileCount trajectory — active climbing count means encryption in progress. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, kill the writing process, block its hash, and snapshot/protect any remaining unencrypted shares and hypervisor datastores. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating SHA256 across the fleet, correlate with the vssadmin norealvolume and /WIPEMODE command-line detections, and check ESXi/Nutanix and NAS telemetry since Anubis encrypts those platforms too.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".anubis"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FolderPath), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 5), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where FileCount > 50
| order by FileCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".anubis"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FileCount > 50
| order by FileCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*.anubis OR *.ANUBIS OR *.Anubis)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.anubis$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(as=fileCount))
| fileCount > 50
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(Filesystem.file_path) as distinct_paths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.anubis" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where distinct_paths > 50
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Filesystem.file_path) as distinct_paths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.anubis" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where distinct_paths > 50
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents

Ernst & Young data breach claimed by ShinyHunters extortion gang

BleepingComputer
2026-07-27 6 use cases 2 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

The ShinyHunters extortion gang has claimed responsibility for a recently disclosed Ernst & Young data breach, saying it obtained credentials for some of the company's systems via a supply-chain attack. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1486
